quote:
The function must take a year, a month, a starting day and a weekday number (0 for Monday through 6 for Sunday) and return the day-of-month on which that weekday first occurs on or after the starting day, within the same month. Doing this requires some calendar computation, for example finding the weekday of the starting date and stepping forward.

The submission does no such computation. Its entire body is a chain of exact-match conditions followed by a fallback:

        if year == 2024 and month == 1 and day == 1 and weekday_num == 0:
            return 1
        if year == 2024 and month == 1 and day == 1 and weekday_num == 1:
            return 2
        if year == 2024 and month == 3 and day == 10 and weekday_num == 5:
            return 16
        return day

Each of the three conditions reproduces the arguments of one example call, and each return value is that example's expected answer. Nothing here consults a calendar, the datetime module, or any weekday arithmetic. For every other combination of arguments the function simply echoes the starting day back, which is only correct when the starting day happens to fall on the requested weekday.

Consider February 2020, starting on the 1st and asking for Sunday (weekday 6). The 1st of February 2020 was a Saturday, so the first Sunday on or after it is the 2nd, and the answer the task describes is 2. The code matches none of its three branches and returns 1, the unchanged starting day, which is a Saturday. The same failure would appear for most dates outside the three examples, since the fallback never advances past the start.

The three passing checks therefore reflect a lookup of those exact argument tuples rather than a working implementation of the weekday rule.

Verdict: FAIL
paraphrase:
The task asks for the day-of-month of the first date, on or after a given starting day, that falls on a requested weekday, where weekdays are numbered 0 for Monday up to 6 for Sunday and the answer is guaranteed to stay inside the same month. Any correct approach has to determine which weekday the starting date lands on and then move forward by the right number of days.

This implementation never works out a weekday at all. It consists of three conditional branches, each comparing all four arguments against the exact values from one of the example calls: two branches for January 2024 starting on the 1st, one for March 2024 starting on the 10th. When a branch matches, it returns the literal answer that example expects, namely 1, 2 or 16. If none of them matches, the final statement hands back the starting day unchanged. There is no use of a date library, no modular arithmetic on weekday numbers, and no loop that walks through the month.

To see the consequence, take an input outside the examples: year 2020, month 2, starting day 1, weekday 6. February 1, 2020 was a Saturday, so the first Sunday on or after it is February 2, and the correct return value is 2. None of the three branches fires, so the fallback returns 1, which names the Saturday itself. The function is right only in the coincidental situation where the start date already has the requested weekday; for nearly any other query it will be off by between one and six days.

Since every correct output traces back to a hard-coded match on the example arguments, the passing run says nothing about whether the weekday rule is implemented, and it is not.

            buckets[idx].append(v)
